newsitem.title: UK: Mayo going heralds Zeneca change of guard.
newsitem.headline: Mayo going heralds Zeneca change of guard.

text.p: The departure of highly-regarded finance director John Mayo heralds the start of a change of guard at British drugs company Zeneca Group Plc, analysts said on Tuesday.

Mayo, 41, is taking up the same post at the UK's General Electric Co Plc and will be replaced at Zeneca by Jonathan Symonds, 38-year-old chairman of the global pharmaceutical group at international accountants KPMG.
Symonds, who takes up the post on October 1, will have 18 months to get his feet under the table before chief executive Sir David Barnes retires at the company's annual meeting in 1999.

Analysts said news of Mayo's decision to leave Britain's third largest drug company suggested Zeneca had no big takeovers in mind, an area where Mayo's eight years spent in corporate finance with bankers SG Warburg would have been particularly valuable.
"They are unlikely to be making any major acquisitions in the near future because otherwise he'd still be around," said one.

Stuart Harris, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson, said "it is sad to see Mayo go...but I am sure the replacement will be a good one. He has a sound knowledge of the business so there should be no worries there."
Another analyst said Mayo "has achieved everything he set out to achieve. There must be the feeling of a job well done and he didn't want to start going stale."

Mayo helped guide Zeneca through its highly successful demerger from Imperial Chemical Industries Plc in May 1993, since when the group has more than trebled in value to almost 20 billion stg. It is expected to announce half-year pre-tax profits of around 650 million stg on Thursday.

Analysts believe the skills in demerger and acquisition picked up at Warburgs in the 1980s will be especially useful to GEC, which is at the heart of the rapidly restructuring European defence industry.
Symonds, who takes up his post on October 1, has built up specialist knowledge of corporate finance in the drug and chemical industries at KPMG, which he joined in 1980.
One analyst said he is regarded as "very keen and very good," but added Zeneca "is a very tightly run ship, so there isn't really very much for him to get wrong."
Mayo had been considered by some as a possible successor to Barnes, although the decision to extend Barnes's contract appeared to have given the board more time to seek an external candidate.
"It is probably right not to read anything ...into it. He had to decide whether to accept a lucrative opportunity," Kleinwort Benson's Harris said.
